ci: tune test parallelism and avoid recursive cache scans (#22463)

## Background

In [the failing Node 22
job](https://github.com/vercel/ai/actions/runs/37952296361/job/113895352240),
four mocked Z.AI and DeepInfra tests exceeded the five-second timeout.
Turbo ran 16 packages concurrently, each with its own Vitest worker
pool. On the four-CPU runners we measured, Vitest defaults to three
workers per package.

The initial PR workflow also spent over 18 minutes resolving example
cache paths before archiving began. The recursive globs follow pnpm
dependency symlinks, despite the example workspaces being limited to
`examples/*`.

## Summary

- Run at most one package per available CPU (`--concurrency=100%`) and
cap each package at two Vitest workers. On a four-CPU runner, this
reduces the maximum Vitest worker count from 48 to 8 while retaining
file parallelism and the existing test timeouts. Individual package
tests keep their normal local parallelism.
- Include `VITEST_MAX_WORKERS` and the matrix Node major in Turbo's test
environment and cache key so worker configuration reaches the package
tasks and cached results cannot cross Node majors.
- Match example build caches at the workspace-directory level, avoiding
recursive scans through dependency symlinks.
- Document the CI concurrency configuration in the testing guide.

## Validation

The [final PR
workflow](https://github.com/vercel/ai/actions/runs/37970581255) passed
all 49 jobs, including the full package suite on Node 22, 24, and 26 (79
tasks, 25,562 passing test executions, zero cached tasks for each Node
version), all example builds, the docs build, full type checking, and
lint/format checks.

The initial [PR
workflow](https://github.com/vercel/ai/actions/runs/37960649691) passed.
We then compared eight package/worker layouts on GitHub's four-CPU
`ubuntu-latest` runners, pinning revision
`897e930dcfbad27bcfe44b45b935aa2599ac83de` and reusing the same build
artifact. Every timed command ran the full 79-task package suite with
Turbo cache reads disabled: 25,562 passing test executions per run.

Fresh-runner comparisons exposed substantial hardware and runner
variation, so the [final
comparison](https://github.com/vercel/ai/actions/runs/37967631187)
rotated the original setting and the two finalists across the same Node
22 runners. Node 24 and 26 compared both finalists in opposite orders.

Chosen setting: **four packages × two workers** on a four-CPU runner.

| Node 22 runner | Original: 16 packages × default workers | Selected: 4
packages × 2 workers | Test-time reduction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 248.62s | 220.03s | 11.5% |
| 2 | 244.73s | 215.56s | 11.9% |
| 3 | 208.68s | 192.91s | 7.6% |

The selected layout also beat the six-worker finalist (two packages ×
three workers) in all seven same-runner comparisons across Node 22, 24,
and 26, by 2.7–5.0%. The smaller layout used somewhat less CPU time, but
did not improve test duration. All **41 full-suite benchmark executions
passed without timeouts**, including all three supported Node majors.

Earlier experiments: [initial
layouts](https://github.com/vercel/ai/actions/runs/37963301128), [paired
finalists and serial
packages](https://github.com/vercel/ai/actions/runs/37964403303), and
[six-worker
layouts](https://github.com/vercel/ai/actions/runs/37966198146). Timings
measure the test command, excluding installation, builds, and cache
uploads. These are measurements of the tested layouts, not a guarantee
of the same improvement on every runner.

The cache-path change was checked with the exact versions used by
`actions/cache` (`@actions/cache` 6.1.0 and `@actions/glob` 0.6.1). On
the installed local workspace, the recursive scan had not finished after
20 seconds; the narrower scan completed in 6.7ms. A fixture with Next.js
and Angular caches plus a workspace dependency symlink confirmed that
the new paths retain the intended caches and exclude the duplicate
dependency path. Changing the path patterns changes the cache version,
so the first CI run rebuilds the example caches. In the [latest PR
workflow](https://github.com/vercel/ai/actions/runs/37970581255), all
four example builds passed and saved their caches in 1–5 seconds. The
other-frameworks shard fell from 18m22s to one second, including archive
creation and upload.

Full TypeScript checking including examples and repository lint/format
checking passed. Workflow YAML parses, and Turbo dry runs produce
different test-cache keys for Node 22 and 24. This changes CI
configuration and contributor documentation, so no published-package
changeset is needed.

feat(azure): support MAI-Voice-2-Flash and MAI-Voice-2 speech (#21851)

> Stacked on the MAI-Transcribe-1.5 PR (#21850). Review that first; this
PR's diff is only the speech changes.

## Background

MAI-Voice (Microsoft AI's text-to-speech family) is served through Azure
Speech, not the Azure OpenAI `/audio/speech` API. There's no model
field. The model is a suffix on the SSML voice name
(`en-US-Harper:MAI-Voice-2`), and the request body is SSML posted to
`/tts/cognitiveservices/v1`. `azure.speech()` only supports OpenAI TTS
deployments today.

## Summary

- `azure.speech()` now returns a model that picks the API per request,
the same way `azure.transcription()` does. `mai-voice-2-flash` and
`mai-voice-2` (case-insensitive) use Azure Speech by default. Other IDs
keep using OpenAI. `providerOptions.azure.api` overrides the choice and
also passes through AI Gateway.
- The new SSML speech model:
- `voice` is a locale-prefixed voice ID (default `en-US-Harper`). The
model's Azure name is appended; full names containing `:` are sent
unchanged. `xml:lang` comes from the voice locale.
- `outputFormat`: `mp3` (default), `wav`, `pcm`, and `opus` shorthands,
plus any native `X-Microsoft-OutputFormat` value. Other values fall back
to mp3 with a warning.
  - `speed` maps to `<prosody rate>`.
- `providerOptions.azure.style` / `styleDegree` map to
`mstts:express-as`. Styles aren't validated client-side because they
vary by voice and the docs contradict themselves (the documented
`excitement` example returns 400). `styleDegree` without `style`
produces a warning.
  - Text and attributes are XML-escaped, so input can't inject SSML.
- `language` picks a default voice when `voice` isn't set (15 languages,
e.g. `de` → `de-DE-Mia`, `es` → `es-MX-Valeria`). Unsupported languages
and `auto` fall back to `en-US-Harper` with a warning. An explicit
`voice` wins; a conflicting `language` produces a warning.
  - `instructions` produces an unsupported warning.
- Azure answers bad voices, styles, and formats with an empty 400. That
becomes a non-retryable `APICallError` with an actionable message. JSON
errors (401) keep Azure's message, and 429/5xx (including 502) stay
retryable.
- TTS reuses the Speech settings added for MAI-Transcribe:
`{speechBaseURL}/tts/cognitiveservices/v1`, defaulting to
`https://{resourceName}.cognitiveservices.azure.com`, with the
`Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key` header and `tokenProvider`. One resource and
one credential cover both families.
- Add `azure.speechModel()` as an alias, so `ProviderV4.speechModel`
consumers (provider registry, hosted Gateway) can create Azure speech
models. Export `AzureSpeechModelOptions`.
- Docs (MAI-Voice section and speech guide rows), two examples, tests,
and a patch changeset.

`MAI-Voice-1` is intentionally not included: the MAI team asked us not
to ship it.

Behavior change: `providerOptions.azure` is now parsed strictly for
every `azure.speech()` model, as it already is for
`azure.transcription()`. Unknown keys throw `InvalidArgumentError`
instead of being ignored. Speech-only keys on OpenAI deployments produce
warnings.

## End-to-End Verification

Live calls against a Foundry Speech resource in `eastus`:

- `examples/ai-functions/src/generate-speech/azure/mai-voice-2-flash.ts`
and `mai-voice-2.ts` (es-MX, wav, speed, style + styleDegree): both
return valid 24 kHz mono audio with no warnings.
- Round trip: the default-voice output of both models, Flash +
`excited`, and Voice-2 + `whispering`/`styleDegree` + speed was
transcribed with MAI-Transcribe-2. Every transcript matched the input
text.
- Output formats: `wav` (audio/wav), `pcm` and
`raw-8khz-8bit-mono-mulaw` (Azure labels both `audio/basic`), `opus`

- Speed: `0.5` vs `2` changes duration on both models.
- Escaping: `Tom & Jerry <3 "quotes"` and an SSML injection string

- `language` without a voice: all 15 mapped languages synthesize on both

- Re-probed error paths after review: unknown voices, 2.1-only voices,

## Background

`run` 2.1.8 added a per-invocation CPU time limit
(`limits.cpuTimeoutMs`, vercel-labs/run#78) that is separate from the
wall-clock `timeoutMs`. It defaults to 10s and fails with
`RUN_CPU_TIMEOUT`.

Because `@ai-sdk/code-mode` depends on `run@^2.0.0`, fresh installs
already resolve a `run` release that enforces this default. Code mode
has no option to configure it, and `RUN_CPU_TIMEOUT` is not mapped.

pins `run@2.0.0`, so CI does not exercise this path.

- Add `executionPolicy.cpuTimeoutMs`. It defaults to `10_000`, matching
`run`, and is passed through to `run` limits.
- Add an exported `CodeModeCpuTimeoutError` (`CODE_MODE_CPU_TIMEOUT`,
`details: { cpuTimeoutMs }`) and map `RUN_CPU_TIMEOUT` to it.
- Translate `limits.cpuTimeoutMs` validation errors to
`executionPolicy.cpuTimeoutMs`.
- Document the difference between `timeoutMs` (wall clock, includes tool
waits) and `cpuTimeoutMs` (sandbox CPU only) in the code mode docs.
- Add tests for the error mapping, for tool wait time not counting
toward the CPU limit, and for option validation.

The version floor is `2.1.8` rather than the latest `2.1.10` because
2.1.9 and 2.1.10 are still inside the repo's 3-day `minimumReleaseAge`
window. The caret range still lets users resolve 2.1.10. The lockfile
can be bumped in a follow-up once those releases mature.

feat(openai): support message-level reasoning effort updates (#21418)

## Why

Applications can preserve prompt caching when changing reasoning effort
during a conversation by appending effort changes while leaving the
earlier prompt prefix unchanged. The SDK already exposes Anthropic's
support through message-level provider options. This PR follows that
pattern for OpenAI's `configuration_update` items.

## Summary

Adds message-level reasoning effort updates through
`providerOptions.openai.reasoningEffortUpdate`:

```ts
{
  role: 'system',
  content: '',
  providerOptions: {
    openai: { reasoningEffortUpdate: 'high' },
  },
}
```

Each message becomes an OpenAI `configuration_update` at the same
position in the input. It uses the existing `allowSystemInMessages`
opt-in. Message-level updates record where reasoning effort changed
during the conversation, so the adapter throws if it cannot preserve

`openai` as a fallback when Azure options are absent.

packages. Azure documentation includes a typed example and explains that
custom deployment names do not enable configuration updates unless the

agent to check the specific workspace package and install with target
package filters (e.g. `pnpm add ai --filter <pkg>`) prevents agents from

## Background

- `useChat({ id })` creates and owns its internal `Chat` instance.
- When the ID changed during an active response, the hook replaced that
instance without aborting it, leaving an unreachable request running.
- Caller-managed `Chat` instances must remain untouched so applications
can intentionally keep inactive threads streaming.

## Summary

- Abort the previous `Chat` only when it was created internally by
`useChat`.
- Preserve externally supplied `Chat` instances when they are replaced.
